Article Title: ‘RR are at the top of the list’: Ashwin makes big revelation on Hardik Pandya trade
Article Text:

Speculation surrounding Hardik Pandya 's future with Mumbai Indians has intensified, with former India spinner Ravichandran Ashwin weighing in on reports linking the star all-rounder with a potential move to Chennai Super Kings ahead of the next Indian Premier League season.Rumours of a possible trade between the five-time champions have gained traction on social media, with suggestions that CSK icon MS Dhoni could personally persuade Hardik to join the Chennai franchise. However, Ashwin believes that while the all-rounder's arrival would strengthen CSK, a deal remains a distant possibility.Speaking on his YouTube channel, Ashwin acknowledged the appeal of having Hardik in the CSK setup but stopped short of endorsing the speculation surrounding the proposed move."There have been conversations that Dhoni will personally convince Hardik Pandya to come to CSK. It will be a great addition for CSK. But in my opinion, it is a real far-shot," said Ashwin.The former India spinner also offered an alternative possibility, claiming that Rajasthan Royals could be better placed to secure Hardik's services if a trade materialises."From what I've heard, RR are at the top of the list in the Hardik trade," he added.Ashwin's comments come at a crucial time for Mumbai Indians, who are preparing for a significant change in their coaching setup following the departure of head coach Mahela Jayawardene.Mumbai Indians confirmed on Saturday that Jayawardene had ended his second spell as head coach after two seasons in charge.The 49-year-old Sri Lankan, who guided the franchise to three IPL titles during his first tenure, returned to the role ahead of the 2025 season after previously coaching MI between 2017 and 2022.His second stint produced mixed results. Mumbai finished fourth in the 2025 season before suffering defeat in Qualifier 2, while their 2026 campaign proved considerably more disappointing, with the five-time champions ending the tournament in ninth place.The franchise must now identify a new head coach with the November 15 IPL retention deadline less than a month away.With a major decision pending in the dugout and trade speculation surrounding Hardik continuing, Mumbai Indians face an important period ahead of the next season.
Article Summary: Hardik Pandya has been linked with a move to Chennai Super Kings. Ravichandran Ashwin believes a deal between CSK and Mumbai Indians is a'real far-shot' The former India spinner also claims Rajasthan Royals are a better option. Mahela Jayawardene leaves Mumbai Indians after second stint as head coach.

Article Title: ‘Massive difference between words and actions’: Ex-India cricketer’s blunt take on Ravindra Jadeja’s snub

Former India opener Aakash Chopra has questioned the selectors’ decision to leave Ravindra Jadeja out of the entire five-match ODI series against New Zealand, pointing to what he sees as a contradiction between the team management’s stated plans and its selection choices.India are scheduled to play five ODIs against New Zealand, beginning in Auckland on November 4. Axar Patel has been preferred over Jadeja as the left-arm spin-bowling all-rounder, despite the Indian think tank previously indicating that Jadeja remains part of its plans for the 2027 World Cup.Speaking on his YouTube channel, Chopra said Jadeja’s absence had not received enough attention and questioned the credibility of the assurances given about the veteran’s future in the team."Ravindra Jadeja not being there is a big thing. Many people haven't spoken about it. You are playing him very little anyway. You said that he is an integral part of our team, that he is part of your 2027 World Cup plans, but it doesn't seem like that, because there is a massive difference being seen in what you say and what you do," he said.Chopra pointed out that Jadeja had featured against the West Indies but was not played in the third match of that series either.The all-rounder has now been left out of both the first three and the final two matches against New Zealand.The former India opener believes Axar may have moved well ahead of Jadeja in the race for a place in the squad for the 2027 World Cup, suggesting the selectors might already have settled on their preferred option."You played him against the West Indies just now, and you didn't play him the third match there either. Here, you have neither picked him for the first three matches nor the last two matches. Axar Patel has run so far ahead in this race that it seems like the selectors have made up their minds about Ravindra Jadeja," he observed.While acknowledging that Jadeja's white-ball numbers have declined, Chopra said the selection pattern appeared to indicate that India were gradually moving away from the experienced all-rounder. He, however, stopped short of declaring whether that was the right decision.Jadeja was not the only selection decision that drew Chopra's attention. The former cricketer also questioned why left-arm spinner Manav Suthar had not been included in India's squad for the two-Test series against New Zealand.Chopra highlighted Suthar's impressive start to his international career, pointing out that the spinner had taken 23 wickets in his first three matches. He also recalled that Suthar was named Player of the Match in his debut game and had been India's leading bowler during the tour of Sri Lanka."Manav Suthar's name is not there. Let that sink in. He has a three-match career in total, in which he was the Player of the Match in the first match. He was the pick of the Indian bowlers in Sri Lanka," he said.Chopra acknowledged that Jadeja remained ahead of Suthar in the pecking order, but wondered whether the younger spinner could have been considered instead of Washington Sundar."I know only one of Jadeja or Manav Suthar can play, and Jadeja is ahead in that race, but you cannot ignore Manav Suthar's 23 wickets in three matches. Could his name have been there in place of Washington Sundar?" Chopra observed.The commentator also stressed that the selectors should speak to Suthar and explain why he had been overlooked after such a promising start. To underline the significance of his returns, Chopra compared taking 23 wickets in three Tests to scoring three hundreds in as many matches.Shubman Gill (C), Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Shreyas Iyer (VC), KL Rahul (WK), Nitish Kumar Reddy, Axar Patel, Naman Dhir, Anshul Kamboj, Gurnoor Brar, Ruturaj Gaikwad, Arshdeep Singh, Ishan Kishan (WK), Mohammed Siraj, Prasidh Krishna* and Kuldeep Yadav.Shreyas Iyer (C), Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Tilak Varma, Ishan Kishan (WK, VC), Nitish Kumar Reddy, Axar Patel, Naman Dhir, Auqib Nabi, Gurnoor Brar, Ruturaj Gaikwad, Arshdeep Singh, Kumar Kushagra (WK), Mohammed Siraj, Yash Thakur and Kuldeep Yadav.Shubman Gill [C], Yashasvi Jaiswal, KL Rahul [VC], Devdutt Padikkal, Rishabh Pant [WK, availability is subject to fitness clearance], Dhruv Jurel [WK], Ravindra Jadeja, Anshul Kamboj, Jasprit Bumrah, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep, Sai Sudharsan, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Washington Sundar, Kuldeep Yadav, Mohammed Siraj.

Article Title: 'You have to wait': Shreyas Iyer explains why Vaibhav Sooryavanshi missed all 5 T20Is against West Indies
Article Text:
Shreyas Iyer and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi

Iyer advises Sooryavanshi to stay patient

Iyer reflects on India's performance

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India captain Shreyas Iyer has backed young batter Vaibhav Sooryavanshi to remain patient and continue working on his game despite not getting a chance to play in the five-match T20I series against the West Indies. The series ended in a 2-2 draw after the rain-hit fifth match in Bengaluru was abandoned.Sooryavanshi did not play in any of the five matches. His last appearance for India was in the Asian Games final against Pakistan. In eight T20Is, the youngster has scored 246 runs at a strike rate of over 186, including two half-centuries.India continued to rely on experienced openers Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma throughout the series. Samson scored 168 runs in five matches, while Abhishek added 145 runs. Both batters registered two half-centuries, making it difficult for Sooryavanshi to find a place in the playing eleven.Speaking after the fifth T20I, Iyer explained that he has been encouraging Sooryavanshi to trust his preparation and stay relaxed instead of worrying about missing out on opportunities."I just keep telling him [Vaibhav Sooryavanshi], you will get your opportunities.If you are consistent with your process, mindset a bit light and not think too much about not getting an opportunity....you have to wait sometimes. We have two fantastic openers who've been consistent throughout," the skipper said.Iyer said India could have achieved a better series result if the bowlers had performed more effectively in the second and fourth matches, when they conceded more than 240 runs. Despite the bowling struggles, he praised the team's batting and acknowledged the West Indies' strong performances."Could have been a different [series scoreline] if we had bowled well in the 2nd and 4th game. Batting has been sensational, execution we fell short. Credit where due, they batted phenomenally well. Kudos to Shai Hope; he was superb. The ability to bounce back even after a loss [among the big plusses]. We were not able to be consistent throughout, so great learning. Even today, the way we went about our batting was outstanding.Gonna be a challenging series in New Zealand now," he signed off.West Indies captain Shai Hope was named Player of the Series after scoring 261 runs in four innings, including two centuries and a half-century, at a strike rate above 190.In the rain-shortened fifth match, India scored an entertaining total after being asked to bat first. Ishan Kishan smashed 30 runs off just 10 balls, while Naman Dhir remained unbeaten on 24 from six deliveries. West Indies bowlers Shamar Springer and Keemo Paul picked up two wickets each.
Article Summary: India captain Shreyas Iyer has backed young batter Vaibhav Sooryavanshi to remain patient and continue working on his game. The series ended in a 2-2 draw after the rain-hit fifth match in Bengaluru was abandoned. India continued to rely on experienced openers Sanju Samson and Abhishek Sharma throughout the series.

The Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) has named a six-member commentary panel for the men’s ODI tri-series involving Pakistan , England and Sri Lanka, scheduled to be played from October 18 to 31, with prominent English commentators Michael Atherton and Nasser Hussain missing from the line-up.The omission comes two months after the duo interviewed Kasim and Sulaiman Khan, sons of jailed former Pakistan Prime Minister and cricket legend Imran Khan, during the Lord’s Test between England and Pakistan in August 2026. The PCB has not provided any reason for their absence from the upcoming assignment.Atherton and Hussain are among the most prominent voices in international cricket commentary and were part of the broadcast team when England last toured Pakistan for a three-match Test series in October 2024.The interview with Imran Khan’s sons, conducted by Atherton and aired by Sky Sports, lasted 18 minutes and raised concerns over the former Pakistan captain’s deteriorating health in prison. Kasim and Sulaiman alleged that the authorities were ‘blatantly trying to kill him’ through neglect and isolation.The broadcast triggered a strong reaction from the PCB, which objected to what it considered the political nature of the segment and filed a formal complaint with Sky Sports.The situation reportedly intensified to the point that the board threatened a player walkout, with Pakistan considering staying off the field for the afternoon session in protest.Sky Sports went ahead with the interview despite the pressure, although Pakistan’s state broadcaster PTV censored the segment. Atherton subsequently addressed the controversy on a podcast with Hussain, defending his involvement and saying the Pakistani state was attempting to ‘airbrush Imran almost out of existence’.For the upcoming tri-series, the commentary line-up features former Pakistan internationals Waqar Younis, Aamir Sohail, Bazid Khan and Urooj Mumtaz, alongside Sri Lanka’s Roshan Abeysinghe and England’s Mark Butcher. Zainab Abbas will serve as the presenter.Younis will join the panel from the second fixture, when Pakistan meet England at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium on October 20. The tournament opens on Sunday, October 18, with Pakistan facing Sri Lanka in Rawalpindi.
Article Summary: The Pakistan Cricket Board has named a six-member commentary panel for the men’s ODI tri-series involving Pakistan, England and Sri Lanka. Michael Atherton and Nasser Hussain are missing from the line-up. The omission comes two months after the duo interviewed Kasim and Sulaiman Khan, sons of jailed former Pakistan Prime Minister and cricket legend Imran Khan. The PCB has not provided any reason for their absence from the upcoming assignment.

Article Title: 'Hardik Pandya is irreplaceable': Sunil Gavaskar believes India should stop searching for a direct replacement for all-rounder
Article Text:
Sunil Gavaskar

Gavaskar wants India to strengthen its bowling

Former India captain Sunil Gavaskar believes India should stop searching for a direct replacement for Hardik Pandya, as the all-rounder brings a unique combination of batting and bowling that is difficult to match.Instead, he advised the team to consider players who can perform different roles while maintaining a strong bowling attack.Gavaskar shared his views after India's five-match T20I series against the West Indies ended in a 2-2 draw. The final match in Bengaluru was abandoned due to rain.Gavaskar suggested that India should play at least four specialist bowlers and use all-rounders as the fifth and sixth bowling options. He warned that selecting too many batters could weaken the bowling unit and cost India matches."We sometimes get a little bit carried away with trying to find a replacement for Hardik Pandya. Hardik Pandya is irreplaceable. If you can't find somebody of his calibre, then go with somebody who will do a slightly different job," Gavaskar said on JioStar.He pointed to Naman Dhir as an example of a player who can contribute with both bat and ball.Dhir scored an unbeaten 24 off just six balls in the rain-hit final T20I."Naman Dhir is doing that job. He's bowling his overs well, and look at the way he batted in this game," he said.Gavaskar also highlighted the importance of backing spin bowlers and helping them maintain confidence, even when they are not regular members of the playing XI."The moment you go with batting up to number eight, you weaken your bowling, and that's where you get beaten," he said.Gavaskar added that the abandoned final denied India a chance to assess their bowling in the shortened match.Former India opener Aakash Chopra also reviewed Abhishek Sharma's performance, saying the left-handed batter was not at his usual best during the series. However, he stressed that inconsistent performances are normal in an aggressive batting approach."In the last game, when he didn't get much strike, he looked a bit scratchy. He didn't get any rhythm at all, and let's discount whatever happened in this game. So, he was a bit below par by his standards in the series, but that is also going to happen."Chopra added that players aiming for strike rates around 200 cannot be expected to score consistently in every match.
Article Summary: India's five-match T20I series against the West Indies ended in a 2-2 draw. The final match in Bengaluru was abandoned due to rain. Sunil Gavaskar believes India should stop searching for a direct replacement for Hardik Pandya.

Article Title: Shai Hope: Hope for history: West Indies skipper on verge of breaking Phil Salt, Babar Azam's world records in 5th T20I
Article Text:
Shai Hope

With the West Indies putting up a stronger challenge than expected, India will need to address some of the flaws in their batting if they are to beat the visitors in the series-deciding fifth T20I in Bengaluru on Saturday. The match is expected to be a high-scoring contest, with the five-match series currently level at 2-2.The run-heavy first four matches have helped hide several weaknesses in India's batting unit, which could come under greater scrutiny in the series decider.West Indies captain Shai Hope , meanwhile, has a chance to break multiple batting records while leading his team towards a series win in India.Hope scored an unbeaten century in the fourth T20I on Wednesday (October 14) and has made 261 runs across the four matches so far. If he scores at least 71 runs at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium on Saturday, he will surpass England opener Phil Salt's record for the most runs in a bilateral T20I series.Salt scored 331 runs in five T20Is during England's five-match series against the West Indies in December 2023. Hope will need a big innings in the final match to go past that mark.Hope already holds the record for the most runs scored in a T20I series against India.He can also set a new mark for the most runs scored by a captain in a bilateral T20I series.If he scores at least 25 runs in the fifth T20I, Hope will move past Pakistan's Babar Azam, who scored 285 runs as captain in seven T20Is against England in 2022. Hope has scored 261 runs as captain in the ongoing series.Another century would also put Hope in a league of his own among captains in T20I cricket. He is currently tied with India's Rohit Sharma, Babar Azam and Adil Butt of Eswatini, with all four having scored three T20I centuries as captains. A fourth century would make Hope the first captain to reach that mark in the format.
Article Summary: West Indies face India in the fifth T20I in Bengaluru on Saturday. The five- match series is currently level at 2-2. The match is expected to be a high- scoring contest. Captain Shai Hope has a chance to break multiple batting records.

Article Title: ‘Series in India brings nothing to West Indies’: Cricket’s bilateral revenue model sparks debate
Article Text:
West Indies tour of India (AP Photo)

How the revenue system changed

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Cricket West Indies (CWI) CEO Chris Dehring has questioned the financial system governing bilateral cricket, explaining how it has contributed to the board’s ongoing financial difficulties. Despite the West Indies currently playing a T20I series against India, Dehring said the Caribbean board would not receive any revenue from the series, even as the hosts stand to earn millions.The T20I series is level at 2-2 following Shai Hope’s century in Hyderabad. Speaking to The Scoop by Wisden Cricket, Dehring explained that the financial model leaves visiting teams without a share of the broadcasting revenue generated by bilateral matches."West Indies cricket receives nothing in this case, because the series is being played in India," said Dehring. "A series that could generate $20 million to $30 million in India brings West Indies cricket no revenue."Dehring traced the problem back to 1997, when nine of the 10 ICC member countries voted to change cricket’s financial model. Before that decision, host nations generally paid visiting teams a guaranteed fee, which sometimes earned the West Indies more than hosting matches at home."To understand how this happened, you have to go back to 1997," he added. "I was fortunate, or unfortunate, to be around when the ICC member countries voted to change the financial model that underpinned world cricket. Until then, West Indies was a very attractive team, and everybody wanted us to tour. We would receive a touring fee, which was often worth more than we could earn by hosting a series in the Caribbean."Under the revised system, the country hosting a bilateral series could retain all the revenue generated from its broadcasting rights. Dehring argued that this created a major imbalance between countries with large audiences and smaller cricketing nations."That meant India could retain the revenues generated by a population of one and a half billion people, while West Indies could retain whatever revenues we could generate in Antigua, with its population of around 100,000, or St Kitts, with around 30,000," Dehring continued."It was palpably unfair. We were outvoted nine to one by the ICC member countries. At the time, I said that this decision had effectively signed the demise of West Indies cricket because it took away our main source of income," he added.
Article Summary: Cricket West Indies (CWI) CEO Chris Dehring has questioned the financial system governing bilateral cricket. The financial model leaves visiting teams without a share of the broadcasting revenue generated by bilateral matches. The West Indies are currently playing a T20I series against India, which the hosts stand to earn millions.

Article Title: ‘I got it late, but I got it’: Told she was too old, Suchika Tariyal went from judo, kurash and ju-jitsu to Asian Games MMA bronze
Article Text:
Suchika Tariyal

Suchika Tariyal

The girl who wanted to learn how to fight

Another sport, another beginning

Suchika

Suchika MMA

When they stopped asking for help

Suchika with her husband Kapil

The 700 grams

Suchika first Indian athlete to win an Asian Games medal in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA)

The gym where Suchika Tariyal trains is modest: a single floor, a makeshift mat, a cage and the equipment needed to prepare for mixed martial arts. It is owned by Vikas Dahiya, an MMA fighter himself. When Dahiya is out of town, the keys are with Tariyal and her husband, Kapil Hooda.The couple have become so invested in the place that it is more than a training facility. It is part of the routine around which they have organised their lives, with Kapil closely watching his wife's preparation and sharing the emotional highs and lows of her career.For years, that routine was built around a goal that kept slipping out of reach. Tariyal moved from one combat sport to another, dealt with selection hurdles, and came close to walking away more than once. The medal she had chased since childhood finally arrived at 36, when she became India's first Asian Games medallist in MMA.“For me, it's more than my life. Because I had a dream since childhood, which has come true today. I mean, I got it late, but I got it. I am very happy about it. I can't believe I have achieved it.I still can't believe it. But I feel like I have to do more. That's what's in my mind.”The bronze was a first for Indian MMA. Tariyal, though, was still thinking about the final she had missed. The semifinal against Singapore’s Hui Hoon Teo went to an additional round and was decided by a weigh-in tiebreak. Tariyal was 700 grams heavier and missed the final.“But I missed a gold medal. I was very sad. I had planned to win gold. But it did not happen. I am very sad about it.”The disappointment was familiar. Her sporting career had been marked by moments when she came close to a breakthrough, only for circumstances to push her towards another route. Judo had been her first sport, followed by kurash and ju-jitsu, before MMA gave her another chance at an Asian Games medal.The medal also carried the memory of a time when she had considered walking away altogether.“I had a desire from my childhood, which I made my life and I didn't achieve - either Commonwealth or Asian Games or Olympics. I wanted to get a medal. I wanted people to know about my struggling life, or how I reached here, or how my family helped me reach here.”Tariyal grew up in Chhawla, near Najafgarh in Delhi, one of four sisters. Her introduction to combat sports came not from a dream of winning medals or building an international career, but from an experience that left her feeling vulnerable as a child.When she was around 12 and sporting a ‘boy cut’, a barber at a salon touched her inappropriately. She returned home without telling her family what had happened, frightened and unsure how to process the incident. The experience stayed with her and eventually shaped her decision to learn how to fight back.“The barber touched me wrongly. I felt very bad. I did not know what was going on. I did not know why this happened to me.”“I did not tell anyone. I did not tell my family. I did not want to go out. I did not want to play. I did not know what to do. I wanted to learn a fighting game, so that if this happens again, I can do it.”Her mother eventually enrolled her in judo. Tariyal had wanted to learn boxing, but she took to judo quickly.“I was crazy about it. I didn't want to study or do anything. I just wanted to play judo. I wanted to give my 100% in judo.”She became an eight-time national judo champion. She won silver at the 2018 Commonwealth Judo Championships, gold at the 2019 edition and gold at the 2019 South Asian Games.Tariyal spent 15 years in judo and tried to qualify for the Olympics, but the Covid-19 pandemic disrupted that pursuit. At the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, she lost the bronze-medal bout in the final seconds.The route to the Asian Games through judo had also become difficult. Ranking requirements made selection challenging, so she turned to kurash, which offered another pathway.She trained for around a year and won the selection trials, but her name was not cleared for the 2023 Asian Games in Hangzhou until the final days before the competition.“Due to two federations, we were left behind. I didn’t have my name on the list. At that time, Mr Anurag Thakur was the sports minister. He helped us a lot. He made us understand. He listened to us. I got my name in the last moment, but I didn’t get enough training because we were running to get my name cleared.”She competed in kurash at Hangzhou but lost.After leaving kurash, Tariyal took up ju-jitsu and became a world champion in 2024. But the achievement did not guarantee a clear path forward, with the sport’s recognition in India remaining an obstacle. MMA offered another route, giving her a fresh opportunity to pursue the Asian Games medal she had long wanted.Pooja Tomar and Himanshu Kaushik encouraged her to try the sport. Tomar is a trailblazer in Indian MMA: she became the first Indian woman to compete in the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) in June 2024, and the first Indian fighter to win a bout in the promotion. Kaushik also guided Tariyal towards the sport.Tomar's presence is not limited to that early advice. She lives one floor above Tariyal and Kapil in their apartment complex on the outskirts of Gurugram. The proximity is part of the small circle around the fighter, a network of people who have encouraged her to continue when other routes have closed.Because of her judo background, she was comfortable with grappling but had to develop her striking. “I am a grappler. I have a judo background. It was difficult for me. I wanted to learn striking,” she said.She gradually worked on the new skills and that transition also opened a route into professional MMA. Tariyal signed a five-fight deal with BRAVE Combat Federation, making her promotional debut at BRAVE CF 92 in Bahrain in December 2024.The deal offered a way to continue competing professionally while she pursued the Asian Games pathway. Tariyal said she had completed two fights under the contract, with three remaining. Her judo background also shaped her choice of traditional MMA for the Asian Games, where the use of a gi (Judogi) and the emphasis on grappling and throws suited her strengths.Tariyal's career has involved repeated reinvention and each change required her to adapt her training and start again, often without the certainty that the new discipline would bring the medal she wanted. But the setbacks were not only about results or injuries. As she grew older, she began hearing a different kind of criticism: that she was too old to continue.Kapil, who works in Manesar, had seen how much Tariyal had given to sport. By the time they married, she had a job and a home, but years of chasing a major medal had left her close to giving up. Kapil urged her to continue, even as the financial burden of keeping her career going grew.“My husband had faith in me. I had given up. I was married and had a good job. I had a house and a husband. Then he believed in me, that I can do it. ‘I have seen you doing it,’” Tariyal said.Keeping her career going cost money. She took unpaid leave from work to train and compete, while overseas camps and travel had to be paid for without any guarantee of a result.“He spent from his pocket, took loans and he trained me. He sent me to Bali. I went there three-four times for two months. I have a job, and when I go for training, I go without pay. I don't get paid. Whatever I needed, he spent it.”Kapil approached people for financial help, but was repeatedly told that Tariyal was too old to continue. Eventually, he stopped asking and concentrated on doing what he could himself.Tariyal also looked for ways to find sponsors. During COVID-19, she appeared on reality television, hoping the exposure might help fund training and competition.“I thought if I do two-four events, I might get a sponsor,” she said. “If I get a sponsor, I will do it.”However, she dislocated her elbow during one of the shows. The injury put her preparation for the 2022 Commonwealth Games at risk. Even though she recovered in time to compete, she decided not to return to reality shows until she had achieved her sporting goals.“I decided I won't go to such reality shows until I achieve. I have to focus on my work,” she said.The doubts about her age continued. Tariyal said she heard at training camps that she should step aside and give younger athletes a chance.“A lot of people meet me and say that you have become so old. You have become 30 years old. You can’t play [the sport],” she said. “We still get to hear in the camps that you are too old. You shouldn't play now. You should drop now. You should give a chance to the youth ahead. So, I have heard this many times.”Her response was to keep competing. “As long as my body is working or I want to play, I can play. And you have seen that I have won a medal,” she said. “The more demotivating people I met in my life, the more motivated I got.”When she moved into MMA, Tariyal said, the federation - MMA-SFI (Mixed Martial Arts Sports Federation of India) - helped with training, food and other requirements and allowed her to use its gym without monthly fees.“I haven't seen such a federation,” she said.She credits Kapil with helping her stay in sport long enough to reach the Asian Games podium. “I would like to thank him. That's why I reached here. It was his dream, which I fulfilled.”At Aichi-Nagoya, the pressure of the opening bout was clear to Tariyal. She admitted to her coach that she was scared, only for him to tell her that he felt the same way, but believed she would do well.“I was very nervous at that time. I told my coach that I was scared. He said, ‘It's fair. You are scared, so you are telling the truth.’ I said, ‘Yes, I am scared.’ He said, ‘It's okay, I am scared too. But you will do well. I know you have worked very hard.’”She focused on winning the quarterfinal and securing a medal. “I had a belief that I have to win this round. Only then I will be able to secure a medal. I played all out. I don't know how I performed in the first round. I was very disturbed. Will my body work or not? What kind of performance will come? I played and I won. I was very happy.”The win assured her of bronze. The semifinal tiebreak kept her out of the final by 700 grams. At 36, Tariyal had finally won the Asian Games medal she had wanted since childhood.For now, Tariyal’s focus shifts to the World Championships in November. She will travel to Mumbai to prepare for the event, while the two remaining bouts on her BRAVE Combat Federation contract remain on the back burner.
Article Summary: Suchika Tariyal is the first Indian athlete to win an Asian Games medal in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) The 36-year-old missed the final because she was 700 grams heavier. Her introduction to combat sports came not from a dream of winning medals, but from an experience that left her feeling vulnerable.

Article Title: China’s stapled visa row costs Arunachal weightlifter shot at World Championships
Article Text:
India China

New Delhi: Another sporting flashpoint in India-China ties has cost weightlifter Charu Pesi a shot at the world stage, with the Indian Weightlifting Federation (IWLF) withdrawing the Arunachal Pradesh athlete from the upcoming Senior World Weightlifting Championships in Ningbo after Chinese authorities indicated that he would be issued a stapled visa.Sources told TOI that the Chinese Visa Application Service Centre (CVASS) here sought an undertaking from the Indian federation confirming Pesi’s acceptance of the visa.The IWLF consulted government officials, who maintained that India does not recognise stapled visas issued by China to residents of Arunachal Pradesh. The federation subsequently decided against sending the men’s 65kg lifter to the championships, which begin on Oct 24.An eight-member Indian squad, led by Olympic medallist Mirabai Chanu , is scheduled to compete in Ningbo, with visa processing for the rest of the contingent continuing as usual.Unlike a regular visa stamped on a passport, a stapled visa is issued on a separate piece of paper. Beijing’s practice of issuing such visas to Arunachal Pradesh residents reflects its refusal to recognise India’s sovereignty over the region. India has consistently rejected the practice, viewing it as a challenge to its territorial integrity.This is far from an isolated incident. In July 2023, three Arunachal Pradesh wushu athletes, Nyeman Wangsu, Onilu Tega and Mepung Lamgu, were issued stapled visas for the Summer World University Games in Chengdu. India protested and withdrew its entire wushu contingent.The dispute resurfaced ahead of the Hangzhou Asian Games later that year, when the athletes faced entry and accreditation hurdles, preventing them from competing.For the lifter, it is a bitter setback. The championships would have offered valuable international exposure, with crucial ranking points at stake in the qualification race for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Article Summary: Charu Pesi will not compete at the Senior World Weightlifting Championships in Ningbo. Chinese authorities indicated that he would be issued a stapled visa. Beijing’s practice of issuing such visas to Arunachal Pradesh residents reflects its refusal to recognise India's sovereignty.

Article Title: Sonipat’s golden harvest: How Haryana city became India’s medal factory
Article Text:
Sonipat’s golden harvest: How a Haryana city became India’s medal factory

Neha

Pritam Rani

who was with BSF

Kiran Pahal

1,000-plus

20%

The Sonipat story

Poll Vote & Share your view What role should government and institutions play in supporting young athletes? Provide funding and scholarships Create more training facilities Organize local competitions 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Sonipat's Winners

Sonipat’s Gold Medal Winners [13]

When Kushal Dalal picked up boxing gloves, his family didn’t say no. When he gave that up and decided on archery – because Kushal didn’t like the idea of hitting anyone and felt at home in “a peaceful sport” – they agreed to that, too. There was no place around to practise archery, so a section of the family’s 5-acre farmland at Siwanka village in Sonipat was cleared. Paddy straw was woven to give him targets.Village gossip had brought Kiran Pahal’s running days to an abrupt end. After talk of Kiran “speaking to a boy” reached her father, he stopped her from going out. He relented after Kiran went on a hunger strike. Her grandmother used money from her pension to buy her a pair of running shoes.Before Neha Goyal played hockey for India, she helped her mother and sisters fix bicycles. Neha was eight when a friend told her hockey players got free shoes, clothes and notebooks. Her mother, who worked in houses and at a foam factory, didn’t stop her from playing.At the recently concluded Asian Games in Japan’s Aichi-Nagoya, a neighbour of Delhi reaped possibly India’s biggest harvest for a single city. Each of these stories – and 10 more like these – culminated in a gold medal.Each began, and blossomed, in Sonipat.Though in NCR, Sonipat doesn’t have Delhi’s influence, Gurgaon’s money or Noida’s infrastructure. As a manufacturing hub of auto components and ancillaries that are used in the domestic market and abroad, Sonipat has so far been writing its script, literally, in parts.Sport, which bubbles in its DNA, works much in the same way – many individual parts that don’t get to show their prowess as a sum. Aichi-Nagoya was that rare instance when they did. Serendipity? Perhaps. Organisation? Possible. Talent? Certainly.But talent needs spotting. And for virtually all the gold medallists, that was someone in the family who made it possible, sometimes with a push, sometimes with a quiet sacrifice –a family clearing land, a grandmother spending her pension, a mother working to buy shoes, a coach paying school fees for a stranger’s daughter.The other aspect of the Japan feat that places Sonipat apart from traditional sporting nurseries like Bhiwani (boxing) is the diversity of the 13 (individual and team combined) gold medals that athletes from here won, across disciplines like hockey, archery, kabaddi , athletics and wrestling.Serendipity did play a part. For several of these medallists, sport wasn’t the original dream. Neha Goyal, midfielder in the gold-winning women’s hockey team, started going for hockey classes after a friend told her hockey players received free shoes, clothes and notebooks. She joined because her family needed those things. Some families saw sport as a way to support the child’s education; others came to see it as a route eventually to a govt job.Coaches TOI spoke to said access to proper training remains the difference between a talent lost and a talent realised. Sonipat’s sportspersons have certainly benefited from its concentration of sports institutions and training centres around Rai and Bahalgarh. It has a Sports Authority of India (SAI) National Centre of Excellence, a residential sports school and Sports University of Haryana . The SAI centre covers 83 acres and its listed facilities include a 70-metre archery field, a floodlit synthetic athletics track, synthetic hockey fields, two mud kabaddi courts, wrestling halls, a sports injury and rehabilitation centre, a hypoxic chamber and hostels.Motilal Nehru School of Sports at Rai, founded by Haryana govt in 1973, has athletics, archery, weightlifting, wrestling and swimming among its competencies.Village akharas, kabaddi nurseries and private academies sit in different parts of the access route. One such academy, run by former India hockey captain Pritam Rani Siwach and her husband, has produced a steady stream of national hockey players. Seven hockey players from Sonipat were part of the men’s and women’s Indian teams that won gold at Aichi-Nagoya: four women and three men. All four women and one in the men’s team (Pritam Rani’s son Yashdeep) trained at the academy, which now has around 200 players, 150 of them girls.Among the youngest there is Ritika. The five-year-old is still mastering her numbers and alphabets in school but is quickly picking up dribbling and promptly agreed to show this reporter the right grip for the hockey stick. “Aise pakadte hain. Aur phir ball ko goal mein daalna hota hai. Jo ball andar daalega, woh jeetega! (this is how you hols the stick. The objective is to score a goal with the ball. Whoever does that wins)” she said.When Pritam Rani started the academy in 2004, she had seven trainees. When the academy paid school fees and helped buy shoes and other equipment, more began to join. I never wanted money to become the reason a talented girl stopped playing,” she told TOI. Food mattered, too. Many girls came from families for whom milk and fruit were luxuries, so the academy began providing soaked chana, milk and bananas.Neha, who came for the shoes, stayed for the dream – of building a house for her mother. “I did not start playing hockey thinking I wanted to play for India. I was in Class IV when a friend told me about the shoes, clothes and notebooks,” she said. “There were people who told my mother to keep me at home. But she never stopped me.” A cash prize for being player of the match changed her attitude towards hockey. “That Rs 2,000 changed something inside me. I started thinking if I played well, I could earn. Then on, hockey was not just a game for me. It became my responsibility,” she said.Abhishek Nain’s first reason for playing hockey was less ambitious. He was nine when he followed a classmate to a ground because it was an excuse to bunk. His father,, asked him to consider quitting hockey – which he was playing at the national level – after a series of injuries and focus on getting a govt job. Coaches persuaded the family to let him continue. Years later, at Aichi-Nagoya, he would score India’s winning goal against Pakistan in the Asiad semi-final.Seeing girls running on a track outside her school drew Kiran into athletics so much that she began sprinting in her school shoes and slippers, sometimes even barefoot. “I did not know where this would take me or that I would one day be wearing the India badge. I just liked running and wanted to try.” She joined Indian Railways in 2021, gaining financial stability after years of training. “For an athlete, knowing that there is a secure job gives a lot of confidence,” said Kiran, who won the 4x400m relay team gold in Japan.Meenu Beniwal, president of Haryana Olympic Association, linked Sonipat’s sporting culture to shrinking landholdings and search for livelihoods beyond farming. “As ancestral landholdings have shrunk and farming has become less viable for many families, sports have emerged as an important pathway to secure govt jobs and build a better future,” she said. Proximity to Delhi and recruitment opportunities in the Army, Railways, paramilitary forces and other central government departments have also encouraged young people to pursue sport, she felt.Sports University of Haryana vice-chancellor Ashok Kumar said ambitious parents have helped build the ecosystem by investing their own money and taking risks for their children. Institutions have added to that support, creating a baseline sporting infrastructure framework in the city. The university admitsstudents each year, and Sonipat accounts for aroundof admissions.Kabaddi player Pardeep Narwal says children in villages such as Rindhana grow up watching neighbours, relatives and seniors succeed in the sport. Local grounds and kabaddi academies run by former players bring large numbers of youngsters into the sport. In Rindhana alone, around 300 children practise across three grounds, he said.“From my village alone 25-30 athletes have played in Pro Kabaddi League,” Narwal said. Seeing other athletes succeed encourages more children in the village to try. “Family members motivate the kids. They look at a neighbour’s son succeeding and ask their own children why they can’t do the same,” he said.Wrestler Naveen Mor describes the same process in akharas, with local dangals giving children competitive experience early. “When an entire community encourages a sport, the chances of producing champions naturally increase,” said Mor, who runs a wrestling academy on a one-acre plot near Murthal, where he trains 70-80 children. He said he does not charge them because talent may emerge from families unable to afford expensive coaching.“Many of our athletes come from humble farming families, where children grow up helping with physical work and learn discipline, endurance and the value of hard work early in life. Wrestling also offered generations of youngsters from middle-class families a way to build a career, earn recognition and secure a govt job.Earlier, choices for many such families were limited, and sports became a route to a better future. Over time, this created a strong sporting culture, with akharas, coaches, families and former wrestlers all contributing to the next generation,” Mor said.The same may now be happening for hockey and athletics. Maybe, it takes a village to keep producing gold medallists.Women’s HockeyNeha GoyalJyotiSakshi RanaShilpi DabasMen’s HockeySumitAbhishek NainYashdeep SiwachAthleticsKiran PahalArcheryKushal DalalKabaddiSunil KumarAshu MalikRajraniWrestlingSujeet Kalkal
Article Summary: Sonipat, in Haryana, won 13 gold medals at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. The city is a manufacturing hub of auto components and ancillaries that are used in the domestic market and abroad. For virtually all the gold medallists, that was someone in the family who made it possible.

Article Title: Three Jharkhand players in India squad for historic lawn bowls series against New Zealand
Article Text:

Kolkata: Three players from Jharkhand will be part of India’s four-member lawn bowls squad for a historic three-Test series against New Zealand in Nov, part of the centenary celebrations of sporting ties between the two countries.Lawn bowls is one of the only four sports, alongside cricket, hockey and football, selected for the centenary programme.2022 Commonwealth Games silver medallists Dinesh Kumar and Sunil Bahadur and rising player Reshma Kumari, all from Jharkhand, have been selected alongside Arjuna Awardee and Commonwealth Games gold medallist Pinki Singh for the series, scheduled from Nov 16-18 in Auckland.“This is a very important event for us because only four sports are taking part in the centenary celebrations. On the days we are playing, no other sport will be taking place, which means we will receive exclusive coverage,” Bowling Federation of India president Ravi Bengani told TOI in an exclusive interview on Thursday.India will play three Test matches over three days, with each Test comprising five matches — men’s pairs, women’s pairs, mixed fours, mixed pairs 1 and mixed pairs 2.The New Zealand series is part of a broader international exposure programme the federation has put in place as it begins preparations for the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad.A 12-member Indian contingent will travel to Malaysia later this month for a World Bowls-sanctioned tournament, while another group will compete in an invitational event in Hong Kong, where Indian players won bronze medals last year.The federation’s confidence has also received a boost from Putul Sonowal’s recent podium finish at the Champion of Champions event, a first for an Indian player at the prestigious competition.“We have decided to participate in as many World Bowls-sanctioned events as possible. International exposure is crucial if we want to bridge the gap with the leading nations,” Bengani said.The federation is also planning to strengthen its support structure through its partnership with Bowls New Zealand. Bengani revealed that India currently does not have a dedicated national coach, making the proposed knowledge-sharing programme particularly significant.“We have signed an agreement with Bowls New Zealand and now we will have more exchange programmes. We will bring their coaches and technical officials to India and provide our players with greater exposure and expertise,” Bengani said.The plans have gained momentum following the federation’s recognition by the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports earlier this year, a move expected to improve funding and access to high-performance support.As far as the 2030 Commonwealth Games are concerned, the federation has set ambitious targets. “I’m committing to at least four gold medals for India in 2030. Personally, I feel we can win even more if we continue on the current path,” Bengani said.With a packed international calendar, plans to bring in New Zealand coaches and technical experts, and Ahmedabad 2030 on the horizon, the federation believes Indian lawn bowls is entering its most ambitious phase yet.
Article Summary: Lawn bowls is one of the only four sports, alongside cricket, hockey and football, selected for the centenary programme. India will play three Test matches over three days, with each Test comprising five matches. The series is part of a broader international exposure programme the federation has put in place as it begins preparations for the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad.

Article Title: EFI mess costs Indian riders global stage, FEI ban from Dec 1
Article Text:
Equestrian Federation of India

New Delhi:

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe the governance crisis at the Equestrian Federation of India will negatively impact athletes' futures? Yes, definitely No, it won't 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Yet another tale of administrative chaos and athletes paying the price. Caught in a prolonged governance crisis at the Equestrian Federation of India (EFI), Indian riders now face a ban from international competitions, with their sporting futures hanging in the balance. The latest setback comes at a time when the govt is pushing to bring more international events to India and widen Indian athletes’ exposure to global competition.The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) has decided to suspend the EFI from Dec 1 over prolonged governance irregularities and failure to hold fresh elections, effectively shutting Indian riders, officials, trainers and horses out of international events. TOI is in possession of FEI’s Oct 15 letter confirming the decision, which was taken at the international body's board meeting on Oct 13.Explaining its move, the FEI said the EFI’s prolonged governance crisis had reached a tipping point. “The absence of elections to date to elect a new Executive Committee, has resulted in a prolonged governance and leadership irregularity that is no longer sustainable,” the letter by FEI Governance Director Francisco Lima stated.The crisis follows the Delhi high court’s dissolution of the EFI executive committee in Feb 2026. Its elected tenure had expired in Sept 2023, while fresh elections remain pending nine months after the court’s intervention. The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) constituted an ad hoc committee on March 27 to oversee the federation and facilitate the electoral process.While acknowledging the committee’s Sept 27 submission and its work, the FEI said elections were expected by Jan 31, 2027. However, the suspension will be reviewed only after the polls are held and evaluated by the international body.The consequences are sweeping. Citing its statutes, the FEI said the EFI “may not attend or be represented at any session or meeting of any FEI body, nor may it organise international events.” More damagingly, athletes, officials, trainers and horses “may not participate in international events organised by the FEI or any other national federation, whether under the Indian flag or the FEI flag.”With the suspension taking effect before the stated election deadline, Indian riders risk losing crucial international competition opportunities. Their return will depend on the completion of elections and the FEI’s subsequent evaluation, leaving athletes caught in a governance crisis they did not create.
Article Summary: The International Equestrian Federation (FEI) has decided to suspend the EFI from Dec 1 over prolonged governance irregularities and failure to hold fresh elections. Indian riders now face a ban from international competitions, with their sporting futures hanging in the balance. The latest setback comes at a time when the govt is pushing to bring more international events to India and widen Indian athletes' exposure to global competition.

Article Title: SA vs AUS: Steve Smith cleared of concussion after helmet blow, returns to field in Durban Test

Former Australia captain Steve Smith has been cleared of concussion and resumed fielding duties on the fifth day of the first Test against South Africa at Kingsmead in Durban on Tuesday, after undergoing a series of clinical assessments following a blow to the helmet.The 37-year-old batter was struck by a short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje during Australia's second innings. Smith attempted to duck under the ball but misjudged its trajectory as it failed to rise as much as he expected.Although he continued batting after the incident, scoring 27 off 41 balls before being caught at long-on off Simon Harmer, Smith did not take the field when South Africa began their second innings on Monday. Michael Neser served as his substitute fielder during that session.However, Smith returned to the field on Tuesday morning after being cleared under Cricket Australia's concussion protocols. He was stationed in the slip cordon when South Africa resumed their chase and subsequently took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling."Steve Smith has undergone a series of clinical assessments over the past 24 hours in accordance with Cricket Australia’s concussion protocols and has been cleared to take the field this morning," Cricket Australia said in a statement.The incident brought back memories of Smith's previous concussion scare during the 2019 Ashes in England, when he was struck on the head by fast bowler Jofra Archer and forced to miss part of a Test match.Smith's return to the field came after medical assessments over the preceding 24 hours, with Australia following the prescribed protocols before allowing the experienced batter to resume his duties.His presence was a boost for Australia as they pushed for victory in the series opener, with South Africa mounting a determined resistance on the final day.South Africa resumed at 102/4 on Tuesday, needing another 319 runs to win. They reached 166/6 by lunch after Australia struck twice to strengthen their grip on the contest.Opener Aiden Markram led the home side's resistance, remaining unbeaten on 69 at the interval alongside Marco Jansen on seven. The pair had to rebuild after Wiaan Mulder's patient 69-run fifth-wicket partnership with Markram ended when Josh Hazlewood had Mulder caught behind by Alex Carey.Part-time spinner Matt Renshaw then dismissed Verreynne, who made just one before edging a reckless shot to Smith at slip.Renshaw has been Australia's standout performer with the bat, having scored 190 in the first innings and 82 in the second, before adding two wickets to his match contribution.Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test. The second Test of the series is scheduled to begin in Gqeberha on Sunday.
Article Summary: Steve Smith cleared of concussion after blow to the helmet. Former Australia captain was struck by short-pitched delivery from Anrich Nortje. Smith took a catch to dismiss Kyle Verreynne off Matt Renshaw's bowling. Australia needed four more wickets at lunch to seal victory in the opening Test.

Article Title: ‘No option but to bat at 5 or 6’: Tilak Varma on adapting to new role in India’s T20I setup
Article Text:
Bengaluru: India's Tilak Varma (PTI Photo)

Tilak working on his finishing skills

Busy schedule no excuse, says India vice-captain

Tilak highlights positives from West Indies series

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India vice-captain Tilak Varma has acknowledged that moving away from his preferred No. 3 position to bat lower down the order presents a challenge, but the 23-year-old is confident that regular practice and mental preparation will help him adjust to the demands of his new role.Tilak has increasingly been used at No. 5 and 6 in T20Is as India continue to settle on their batting combination. While the Hyderabad batter admits that he finds it easier to bat higher up the order, he is focused on becoming a reliable finisher for the team.Speaking after the fifth and final T20I against the West Indies was washed out on Saturday night, Tilak said adapting to different batting positions requires considerable work, particularly when the responsibility is to close out games."It's not that easy to change the numbers from 3 to 5 and 6. It will be slightly challenging. But I have been working on that. How can I finish the games? I have said that I love finishing the games for the country," he said."So, for me as an individual, if you see, it will be easier batting at 3. But unfortunately, now I should bat at 5 or 6 because we have got that combination at the top right now."The left-hander's record at No. 6 offers encouragement. Across nine matches in that position, he averages 65.66 at a strike rate of 195.In 26 combined innings at Nos. 5 and 6, he has scored at an average of 46 and a strike rate of 158.However, the arrival of Ishan Kishan, captain Shreyas Iyer 's presence at No. 4 and the management's decision to continue with the Abhishek Sharma-Sanju Samson opening combination have left Tilak with a reduced role in the middle order.Kishan has been batting at No. 3 and has impressed in the position, leaving Tilak with little choice but to embrace the finishing responsibilities."Kishan is batting at number 3 now, and he is batting really brilliantly there. So, for me now, I think there is no option but to bat at 5 and 6 and do the job for the team."So, I am mentally prepared for that role. And if you see the last few games, I have won from there. So, I am pretty confident to do well there as well," he added.Tilak said he has been putting in extra work in the nets to expand his shot-making range and improve his ability to score quickly when batting with limited time at the crease.He explained that players operating at Nos. 5 and 6 often have only five or six overs to make an impact, making it important to capitalise on scoring opportunities, including when bowlers deliver slower balls within their hitting range."Yeah, we should do that, otherwise, it will be slightly tough. When you go in to bat as a finisher, if a slower one comes into your arc, you should go for 6. Otherwise, if you see in T20, most of the time, if you go into that role of 5 or 6, you will get a maximum of 5 to 6 overs to bat."So, I have changed personally. I have been in this role in my childhood as well. I have got the shots going all over the ground. So, I am confident that if I bat at 3 or 5, I have got the technique to adapt. So, if I practise for 1 or 2 days, I can do any role for the team."Now, if I come back to No. 3, I can adapt after a day or two of practice. I am confident of batting anywhere," he noted.India's players have endured a packed run of fixtures over the past few months, travelling across the United Kingdom, Japan and India. The team will soon head to New Zealand for an all-format tour.Tilak admitted that the demands of consecutive series, different time zones and changing conditions can be difficult, particularly for younger players. However, he stressed that handling such challenges is part of playing international cricket."It will be slightly challenging. But as professional cricketers, we can't give any excuse because when we play back-to-back series, there will be different time zones and all those things. We are used to it now. If you see, for any youngster coming into the team, it will be slightly challenging."But again, you are playing for the country and at the highest level. So, as I said, you should be mentally strong enough to prepare for any challenge, any conditions so that you can become a bigger player," he added.Despite the challenges, Tilak believes India have several encouraging takeaways from the West Indies series that they can carry into the upcoming assignments in New Zealand.He pointed to the team's consistent run-scoring, with India crossing the 200-run mark in every match, as a major positive. He also acknowledged the contributions of Nitish Reddy, Shivam Dube and Naman Dhir."There have been quite a few good things. Especially in the batting, every game we have scored over 200 plus. So, that's a big positive, and that too, we haven't got a proper all-rounder in the team. We have played both Nitish (Reddy) and (Shivam) Dubey as well.But both have done decently well."Then Naman (Dhir) bowled well under pressure. As an off-spinner, bowling to right-handers, and that too against a big-gun team like the West Indies."So, there are a few good points for us to take into the upcoming series. As a team, we have introspected a few things in the bowling as well. So, hopefully, we will do well in the New Zealand series," he said.
Article Summary: India vice-captain Tilak Varma has been used at No. 5 and 6 in T20Is. The Hyderabad batter admits that he finds it easier to bat higher up the order. The 23-year-old is confident that regular practice and mental preparation will help him adjust to his new role.

Article Title: ‘We've matched the defending champions’: West Indies head coach Daren Sammy after 2-2 India T20I draw
Article Text:
BCCI Treasurer Raghuram Bhat presents the series trophy to India's captain Shreyas Iyer and West Indies' captain Shai Hope pose with the series trophy after the fifth and final T20I cricket match was called off due to rain, resulting in a 2-2 series draw, in Bengaluru. (PTI Photo/Shailendra Bhojak)

Sammy sees confidence returning to West Indies

Sammy calls for financial support

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

West Indies head coach Daren Sammy believes his team has taken a major step forward after drawing the five-match T20I series 2-2 against India. The final match in Bengaluru was abandoned due to rain, but Sammy said the team's performances showed that the players are regaining confidence and can compete with the world's best sides.Sammy also highlighted the need for greater financial support to help West Indies cricket grow and maintain its place in international cricket.Sammy said West Indies had entered the series with many people doubting their chances against India. However, the players proved they could challenge the reigning T20 world champions on their home ground."It's a true reflection of how all the teams have played, especially for our guys. I'm pretty sure when the series started, we probably didn't have a chance. But that was just the opinion of others. We would want to win because of something we've not done forever in India, so it would have been nice. I think the cup still is in our favour because we won the home leg the last time we played (in 2023) 3-2,” Sammy told reporters in the post-match press conference.He added that the team's ability to match India and outperform them in certain areas showed how much progress the players had made.“We understand what success means to us; we don't ever take for granted where we are as a team and the challenges that we face. We just look to make those strides, and I think after this series we've taken a massive step. We played against the defending champions, and we've matched them (and) in certain areas we've outplayed them, especially in their backyard,” he added.Beyond the team's results, Sammy stressed that West Indies cricket needs financial backing to secure its future. He pointed to the sport's rich history in the Caribbean and its contribution to fans and businesses around the world.He said the team's recent performances could help attract the support needed to strengthen the regional game.“I think it's important; my mom always says you must have a care factor. No matter what you do in life, the human nature should never lose that care factor. I think we're in a position where we need somebody to put a (hand around the shoulder) of the West Indies cricket.Financially, that is, and series like this, here in India, against the best team in the world, puts us in a conversation closer to that,” he said.Sammy also welcomed the renewed confidence and fighting spirit among his players.“All the guys in the dressing room, they've gone out there and played with intent and I think what was good to see is that the swagger is back, the confidence is back. It started during the World Cup and you could see guys enjoying, and there was a willingness to win. That's where it starts; the belief that we belong where we are, and to have the performances that says you belong there. Hopefully, right now it's just been consistent,” he added.
Article Summary: West Indies drew the five-match T20I series 2-2 against India. The final match in Bengaluru was abandoned due to rain. Head coach Daren Sammy said the team's performances showed that the players are regaining confidence. Sammy also highlighted the need for greater financial support to help West Indies cricket grow.

Article Title: Ranji Trophy: Armed with MS Dhoni’s advice, Kartik Sharma set for captaincy debut
Article Text:
Kartik Sharma (ANI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jaipur: When Kartik Sharma, a young wicketkeeper-batter from Bharatpur district, marked his guard on his red-ball debut two seasons ago, he announced his arrival with authority. He slammed a blistering 115 off 113 balls against Uttarakhand in the Ranji Trophy 2024-25. That initial breakthrough set the tone for a domestic journey built on an unwavering appetite for runs.He truly became elemental to the chatter last year when his explosive six-hitting ability during pre-season trials caught the eye of various IPL franchises, culminating in a Rs14.20 crore contract with the Chennai Super Kings (CSK). Now, at just 20 years of age, he finds himself thrust with the bigger responsibility of leading the senior Rajasthan side. Following left-arm spinner Manav Suthar's departure to New Zealand for India ‘A’ duty, the young 'keeper-batter steps up to lead a side riding high on confidence, having secured three points via a crucial first-innings lead in their opener against Tamil Nadu in Group ‘D’ fixture.Speaking on the eve of the clash against Railways, Kartik opened up about taking over the captaincy reins and said, "I have captained Rajasthan during Under-19 days.I will try to make the team as comfortable as I can. There are a few seniors while most of them are my contemporaries in the side, so I will ensure I remain as humble with them as possible."Kartik’s gritty knock of 42 off 75 balls in the second innings against Tamil Nadu showcased a new dimension to his batting. He credits his high-stakes stint under CSK umbrella for sharpening his match awareness and instilling the patience required to play according to the situationA definitive piece of advice from franchise veteran MS Dhoni has shifted his approach away from brute force toward timing and technical precision. "When I went to Chennai I was a little injured and that is why my batting wasn't going very well. Bhaiya told me to focus on timing. He said that you aren't someone who hits power shots, whatever your timing is, that is your power, so play according to that,” he shared.Kartik has seamlessly integrated this sense of responsibility into his batting, balancing his natural boundary-clearing instincts with a refined technique. “Six-hitting is definitely there, but I am also working on grounded shots and doing my practice for that," he added.Addressing the composition of a dressing room that is decidedly youthful, Kartik sees the clean slate as a strength rather than a setback. "Nothing negative, just the positive is that all are young boys, young blood, so everyone plays together," Kartik stated.Rajasthan enter the fixture holding a distinct psychological edge from their previous outing, while Railways arrive looking to bounce back hard after conceding a first-innings lead to Uttarakhand.For Kartik and his youthful troops, the overarching objective remains focused on the ultimate prize. "The target is to win as many matches as possible," Kartik concluded.
Article Summary: Kartik Sharma is the new captain of Rajasthan in the Ranji Trophy 2024-25. The 20-year-old took over from left-arm spinner Manav Suthar, who is on India ‘A’ duty in New Zealand. The young wicketkeeper-batter made his IPL debut in 2013.

Article Title: Kumar Kushagra’s India call-up gives Jharkhand youngsters a reason to dream
Article Text:
Kumar Kushagra (PTI Photo)

Kolkata:

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Kumar Kushagra’s maiden India call-up has given Jharkhand’s young Ranji Trophy squad another reason to believe, with coach Ratan Kumar hoping the wicketkeeper-batter’s rise to the national side will inspire his teammates to follow suit as they prepare for a challenging away clash against Maharashtra in Pune.Kushagra, initially drafted into the India A squad as Rishabh Pant’s replacement, earned his maiden senior India selection on Friday for the last two ODIs of the New Zealand tour. While Jharkhand will miss the youngster’s services, Ratan believes his achievement can lift the team’s morale.“As a coach, I am feeling top of the world. One boy whom we have been with for 2-3 years, if he is getting a chance for India, the whole team gets a very good feeling,” Ratan told STOI from Pune, ahead of the second-round match.The coach recalled how the news reached the squad after the team arrived in Pune. Kushagra had visited Jamshedpur a few days earlier, when Ratan met him at the hotel, but there had been no discussion about a possible India selection.“When we reached here, the boys got the news. At dinner, everyone was talking about it. Someone told the team, ‘Sir, see, he has got selected.’ The selection came a bit late yesterday, but everyone was very happy,” Ratan said.“The message in the group was that he deserves the place.”For Ratan, Kushagra’s achievement could also inspire Jharkhand’s young squad, whose average age is around 24, to aim for similar honours.“The youngsters and friends get the feeling that I can also do it. Among us, if a player is playing there (for India), everyone gets that feeling inside that we too can go there. So, this is a very good sign,” he added.Jharkhand will look to carry that positivity into their second-round Ranji Trophy Group C fixture against Maharashtra at the MCA Stadium starting Sunday. The visitors began their campaign with three points against Kerala in Jamshedpur after securing a first-innings lead, while Maharashtra opened with a victory over Services at the Palam Ground in New Delhi.The batting unit delivered a strong performance in Jharkhand’s opener, with young opener Shikhar Mohan, captain Virat Singh and Aditya Singh scoring centuries. Utkarsh Singh claimed five wickets in the match, while left-arm spinner Manishi and off-spinning all-rounder Md Kounain Quraishi also made useful contributions.Jharkhand will have another option in the spin department, with experienced all-rounder Anukul Roy returning after his India A assignment. His comeback sets up healthy competition with young Quraishi for a place in the playing XI.“Whoever suits the team’s needs best will be in the eleven. According to the situation, we make players play. It depends on whose skills are needed in that particular match,” said Ratan, emphasizing that selection would be dictated by conditions and team requirements.The red-soil surface at Gahunje could offer some assistance to the pacers, bringing Sushant Mishra and Saurabh Shekhar into focus against a formidable Maharashtra batting line-up.In-form opener and skipper Prithvi Shaw and experienced batter Ankit Bawne will pose a challenge, while the hosts will be further strengthened by the return of regular captain Ruturaj Gaikwad.Ratan, meanwhile, was encouraged by Jharkhand’s all-round showing in the opening game and believes there is scope to build on that performance. “The boys just need to deliver, then definitely we will play very good cricket,” he said.Jharkhand will now look to translate that confidence into another solid performance on the road against a strong Maharashtra side buoyed by its winning start.
Article Summary: Kumar Kushagra's maiden India call-up has given Jharkhand's young squad another reason to believe. Coach Ratan Kumar hopes the wicketkeeper-batter’s rise to the national side will inspire his teammates to follow suit as they prepare for a challenging away clash against Maharashtra.

Article Title: Mahela Jayawardene out! Mumbai Indians look for new head coach ahead of IPL 2027
Article Text:
Mahela Jayawardene (left) and Hardik Pandya

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Mumbai: Mumbai Indians have parted ways with head coach Mahela Jayawardene after another disappointing IPL campaign and are on the lookout for a replacement ahead of the 2027 season.The decision was reportedly taken at a review meeting in August after the five-time champions won just four of their 14 matches in IPL 2026. MI announced on Saturday that the Sri Lankan great would step down ahead of IPL 2027.Jayawardene, 49, was first appointed MI head coach ahead of IPL 2017 and held the position until 2022, overseeing three of the franchise’s five title-winning campaigns, in 2017, 2019 and 2020. He was subsequently elevated to global head of performance as MI expanded into overseas leagues, including SA20, ILT20 and MLC.After a disappointing 2024 season under Mark Boucher, Jayawardene returned as head coach ahead of IPL 2025, guiding the team to Qualifier 2. However, MI struggled in 2026, finishing ninth among 10 teams.MI’s coaching staff currently includes West Indies T20 batting great Kieron Pollard as assistant coach and former India bowling coach Paras Mhambrey as bowling coach. Jayawardene’s exit also comes amid scrutiny of captain Hardik Pandya following another underwhelming campaign.Jayawardene, who captained Sri Lanka to the 2007 World Cup final, expressed gratitude to the franchise and its owners.“Mumbai Indians has been a very special part of my journey for over a decade now. The players, coaching team, the incredible support of the owners and, above all, the fans have made this an experience I will always treasure,” he said.
Article Summary: Mumbai Indians have parted ways with head coach Mahela Jayawardene. MI are on the lookout for a replacement ahead of the 2027 season. The decision was reportedly taken at a review meeting in August. MI won just four of their 14 matches in IPL 2026.

Article Title: Bhuvneshwar Kumar returns after 3 years and 340 days, but rain denies him a moment
Article Text:
Bhuvneshwar Kumar

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bhuvi back where it all began

Bengaluru: It was meant to be a special Saturday, a series decider at the M Chinnaswamy Stadium, which was hosting international cricket after a two-year hiatus. Instead, rain had the final say, turning a high-octane contest into a nine-over shootout before bringing the curtain down on the game and the series.The weather may have won, but not before India’s batters gave the holiday crowd 48 minutes of explosive entertainment, smashing seven sixes and eight fours. With the series locked at 2-2, the rain-hit finale was an anticlimax in a contest where batters had repeatedly dominated and bowlers struggled to keep pace.India captain Shreyas Iyer rued the missed opportunities. “(The series) result could have been different if we had bowled well in the second and fourth games. Our batting was sensational but we fell short in the execution,” he said.After a wait of two hours and 15 minutes, the truncated contest finally got under way, with Ishan Kishan (30; 10b; 3x4; 2x6) leading India’s charge. With the match reduced to nine overs a side, West Indies skipper Shai Hope had little hesitation in opting to field after winning the toss. With just 54 deliveries to make an impression, the Indian batters had no time for caution; the brief was to attack from the outset.Even as a light drizzle threatened to bring the covers back on, India’s batters went after the big shots. The rain returned when the hosts were 118/5 in 7.4 overs, bringing the contest to an abrupt end.Abhishek Sharma kick-started the six-hitting spree with a crisp flick off Keemo Paul that sailed over deep midwicket. He tried to repeat the stroke off the next delivery, only for Shamar Joseph to pluck the ball at midwicket.Ishan needed little time to switch into attack mode. He flicked Romario Shepherd over fine leg for six before finding the gap through midwicket for four. The next delivery brought up the 100th six of the series, as Ishan swept the ball over fine leg and onto the roof, forcing the umpires to call for a replacement ball.Shamar brought the assault to an end by taking pace off the delivery. Ishan failed to connect and holed out to Rovman Powell at mid-on. Skipper Shreyas Iyer chipped in with a 14-ball 22, while Naman Dhir was just warming up with a blistering 24 off six balls when the rain returned.India made two changes to the XI, bringing in Shivam Dube and Bhuvneshwar Kumar in place of Nitish Kumar Reddy, who was ruled out due to illness, and Mayank Yadav.For the 36-year-old Bhuvneshwar, the night marked a return to familiar territory. He made his T20I debut at the same venue against Pakistan in December 2012 and returned to Indian colours after a gap of three years and 340 days, during which India played 106 T20Is.The rain, however, denied him a chance to make his return count.
Article Summary: Rain halts play with India on 118-5 in 7.4 overs. Bhuvneshwar Kumar returns to M Chinnaswamy Stadium for first time in three years. India's batsmen hit seven sixes and eight fours in 48 minutes.

Article Title: 'Success does not necessarily have to be series wins': West Indies captain Shai Hope after rain washes out 5th T20I

Hope reflects on his batting success
